newsitem.title: UK: Clarke criticises UK rate rise, sees more to come.
newsitem.headline: Clarke criticises UK rate rise, sees more to come.

text.p: Former chancellor of the exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Tuesday he would not have acted as his successor, Gordon Brown, did in raising British interest rates to 6.25 percent from six percent two weeks ago.

Speaking during the first debate in Parliament on the economy since Labour won the May 1 election, Clarke predicted base rates would rise at least another half a percentage point because of Brown's "precipitate" action and his accompanying decision to give the Bank of England power over interest rates.

"Moving quickly triggers expectation of further interest rate (rises) to come and the markets will react accordingly to that. Moving too quickly when one has to raise interest rates will almost certainly mean... the eventual peak of interest rate levels will be higher than might otherwise have been the case," Clarke said.
"He's probably ensured that the base rate will eventually go too high. It will go above the 6-3/4 percent (level), which is the highest that I ever moved it to in four years of office," he added.
Clarke argued that the dip in underlying inflation in April to the previous government's target of 2.5 percent showed the recent rate rise was unneccesary on fundamental grounds,

The deflationary effects of sterling's 20 percent rise against the mark over the past year were still working their way through the economy and factory gate prices were dramtically low by historical standards, he said.

Growth in industrial production was extremely subdued and earnings increases remained low -- despite repeated pessimistic predictions to the contrary from the Bank of England and other outside experts, Clarke added.

"He (Brown) acted on the basis that inflationary pressures were building up, and I believe it was a mistake that if interest rates have to move at all he should move so quickly upwards. The signal will have a lasting effect," Clarke said.
"I would not have taken that decision if I had been Chancellor on that day," he added.
